claim: CENP-M is structurally and evolutionarily related to small GTPases.
source: We report that a protein at this interface, CENP-M, is structurally and evolutionarily related to small GTPases but is incapable of GTP-binding and conformational switching.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by structural analysis and phylogenetic studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: CENP-M is incapable of GTP-binding and conformational switching.
source: We report that a protein at this interface, CENP-M, is structurally and evolutionarily related to small GTPases but is incapable of GTP-binding and conformational switching.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by MANT nucleotide binding experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CENP-M is crucially required for the assembly and stability of a tetramer comprising CENP-I, CENP-H, and CENP-K (the HIKM complex).
source: We show that CENP-M is crucially required for the assembly and stability of a tetramer also comprising CENP-I, CENP-H, and CENP-K, the HIKM complex, which we extensively characterize through a combination of structural, biochemical, and cell biological approaches.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by co-expression and purification experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: A point mutant affecting the CENP-M/CENP-I interaction hampers kinetochore assembly and chromosome alignment.
source: A point mutant affecting the CENP-M/CENP-I interaction hampers kinetochore assembly and chromosome alignment and prevents kinetochore recruitment of the CENP-T/W complex, questioning a role of CENP-T/W as founder of an independent axis of kinetochore assembly.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experiments with CENP-ML94A-L163E mutant shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The CENP-M/CENP-I interaction mutant prevents kinetochore recruitment of the CENP-T/W complex.
source: A point mutant affecting the CENP-M/CENP-I interaction hampers kinetochore assembly and chromosome alignment and prevents kinetochore recruitment of the CENP-T/W complex, questioning a role of CENP-T/W as founder of an independent axis of kinetochore assembly.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6C.

claim: CENP-C is the founder of a single pathway of kinetochore assembly, with CENP-H/I/K/M and CENP-T/W as CENP-C-dependent followers.
source: Our studies identify a single pathway having CENP-C as founder, and CENP-H/I/K/M and CENP-T/W as CENP-C-dependent followers.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion, which is supported by depletion experiments shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Kinetochores contain multiple copies of approximately 30 core subunits.
source: They are biochemically complex structures, which contain multiple copies of approximately 30 core subunits, in turn contributing to recruit many additional regulatory proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: CENP-M localizes to kinetochores in both interphase and mitosis.
source: Representative immunofluorescence (IF) images showing endogenous CENP-M localization to kinetochores of HeLa cells in both interphase and mitosis.
evidence: Figure 1B shows immunofluorescence images demonstrating CENP-M localization at kinetochores throughout the cell cycle.

claim: Depletion of CENP-M causes significant chromosome congression defects.
source: HeLa cells depleted for CENP-M display significant chromosome congression defects.
evidence: Figure 1D and 1F show that CENP-M depletion results in chromosome alignment defects.

claim: CENP-M depletion causes robust mitotic arrest.
source: CENP-M depletion also caused robust mitotic arrest, likely a consequence of spindle checkpoint activation caused by chromosome alignment defects (Figure 1G).
evidence: Figure 1G shows quantification of mitotic cells after CENP-M depletion.

claim: CENP-H and CENP-K form a tight dimer when co-expressed in insect cells.
source: CENP-H (known as Fta3 and Mcm16 in S. pombe and S. cerevisiae, respectively [Sanyal et al., 1998; Sugata et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2005]) and CENP-K (known as Sim4 and Mcm22 in S. pombe and S. cerevisiae, respectively [Poddar et al., 1999; Pidoux et al., 2003; Foltz et al., 2006; Okada et al., 2006]) (Figure 2B) form a tight dimer when co-expressed in, and purified from, insect cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel A).
evidence: Figure 2C shows SEC elution profile and SDS-PAGE of the CENP-H/K complex.

claim: Co-expression of CENP-M with CENP-I57–C, CENP-H and CENP-K results in a soluble and stable 4-subunit complex.
source: Indeed, co-expression of CENP-M with CENP-I57–C, CENP-H and CENP-K resulted in a soluble and stable 4-subunit complex that could be purified to homogeneity (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panels C–E).
evidence: Figure 2D shows SEC elution profile and SDS-PAGE of the CENP-HI57–CKM complex.

claim: CENP-M stabilizes CENP-I.
source: Thus, CENP-M stabilizes a quaternary complex containing CENP-H, CENP-I57–C, CENP-K, and CENP-M, to which we refer as 'HIKM complex'.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-expression experiments showing that CENP-I is only soluble when co-expressed with CENP-M, CENP-H, and CENP-K.

claim: The recombinant HIKM complex contains a single copy of each subunit.
source: In SEC experiments, the HI57–CKM complex eluted close to the 158-kDa protein marker (Figure 2D), suggesting that the recombinant complex contains a single copy of each subunit.
evidence: The elution position in SEC is compared to the theoretical molecular mass to infer stoichiometry.

claim: CENP-H and CENP-K interact through an extended interface in a parallel arrangement.
source: Subsequent mass spectrometry analysis identified numerous cross-links between CENP-H and CENP-K, the majority of which mapped to the central domains of these proteins, which are likely to adopt an α-helical arrangement. The specific co-linear distribution of cross-links in this region suggests that CENP-H and CENP-K interact through an extended interface in a parallel arrangement (Figure 2E; the list of crosslinks is available in Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Cross-linking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2E supports this structural arrangement.

claim: The N-terminal region of CENP-I (residues 57–281) binds the CENP-H/K complex.
source: In addition to interacting with each other, the central domains of CENP-H and CENP-K displayed an extensive network of cross-links with the N-terminal region of CENP-I57–C. Accordingly, we were able to reconstitute an interaction between a recombinant segment encompassing the N-terminal region of CENP-I (residues 57–281, which was expressed in a soluble form in the absence of other stabilizing components) and the CENP-H/K complex (Figure 2F), thus confirming that CENP-H/K binds the N-terminal region of CENP-I.
evidence: Figure 2F shows SEC co-elution of CENP-H/K with CENP-I57–281.

claim: CENP-M does not interact with the CENP-H/K complex.
source: We did not observe cross-links between CENP-M and the CENP-H/K complex (Figure 2E), and indeed there was no detectable interaction between these proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel F).
evidence: Figure 2E shows no cross-links between CENP-M and CENP-H/K, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel F shows no SEC co-elution.

claim: CENP-M interacts with CENP-I.
source: Two cross-links, however, were observed between CENP-M and CENP-I (Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2E shows cross-links between CENP-M and CENP-I.

claim: The incorporation of CENP-M in the CENP-HIKM complex requires CENP-I residues C-terminal to residue 281.
source: In SEC experiments, CENP-M did not interact with CENP-I57–281 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel G) or with the CENP-HI57–281K complex (Figure 2G), collectively suggesting that the incorporation of CENP-M in the CENP-HIKM complex requires CENP-I, and that the interaction of CENP-M with CENP-I requires residues located C-terminally to residue 281.
evidence: Figures 2G and 2—figure supplement 1, panel G show that CENP-M does not bind CENP-I57–281 or the CENP-HI57–281K complex.

claim: CENP-I bridges CENP-H/K and CENP-M.
source: In summary, these observations suggest that CENP-I bridges CENP-H/K and CENP-M, and that both CENP-H/K and CENP-M contribute to CENP-I solubility and stabilization.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the biochemical reconstitution and cross-linking data presented.

claim: The structure of CENP-M1–171 consists of a five-stranded parallel β-sheet surrounded by six α-helices.
source: The structure of CENP-M1–171 is globular and consists of a five-stranded parallel β-sheet surrounded by six α-helices (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel B).
evidence: The crystal structure of CENP-M1–171 was determined and is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CENP-M is structurally related to small GTPases.
source: A search of the Protein Data Bank (PDB) using the Dali server (Holm and Rosenström, 2010) indicated that CENP-M is structurally related to small GTPases (for comparison, the structure and topology of the small GTPase Rab1 are shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel C, respectively), as previously predicted in a bioinformatics analysis (Santaguida and Musacchio, 2009; Westermann and Schleiffer, 2013).
evidence: Structural comparison using the Dali server identified small GTPases as the closest structural homologs.

claim: CENP-M lacks essential sequence motifs required for GTP binding and hydrolysis.
source: A sequence alignment derived from the structural superposition of HsCENP-M with HsRab1A (PDB code 4FMC, [Dong et al., 2012]) shows that CENP-M has lost essential sequence motifs required for GTP binding and hydrolysis by small G-proteins (Vetter and Wittinghofer, 2001; Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows a sequence alignment highlighting the absence of key GTPase motifs in CENP-M.

claim: The P-loop of CENP-M lacks two essential Gly residues.
source: For instance, the glycine-rich P-loop (GX4GKS/T, where X is any aminoacid), which is involved in GTP binding by GTPases, lacks two essential Gly residues in CENP-M.
evidence: Figure 3C shows the sequence alignment indicating the absence of these glycine residues.

claim: The switch I and switch II regions of small GTPases are profoundly modified in CENP-M.
source: The so-called switch I and switch II regions of small GTPases, which are sensitive to nucleotide hydrolysis and create a dependency on nucleotide status for the interaction of GTPases with their effectors (Vetter and Wittinghofer, 2001; Cherfils and Zeghouf, 2013), are also profoundly modified in CENP-M.
evidence: Figure 3C shows the structural and sequence differences in these regions.

claim: CENP-M does not bind GTP, GDP, ATP, or ADP.
source: Thus, HsCENP-M has the fold of a small GTPase, but may be unable to bind (and therefore hydrolyze) GTP. Experiments with MANT nucleotides (Hiratsuka, 1983) confirmed this prediction directly (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel D).
evidence: Figure 3D shows MANT nucleotide binding experiments demonstrating no binding to CENP-M.

claim: CENP-M family members cluster at the base of the RAB/RAS sub-families in phylogenetic analysis.
source: CENP-M family members cluster at the base of the RAB/RAS sub-families, suggesting that CENP-M might have originated at a similar time.
evidence: Figure 3E shows a phylogenetic tree with CENP-M sequences clustering near RAB/RAS families.

claim: CENP-M has been lost from most fungi.
source: CENP-M, however, has been lost from most fungi, where additional protein products of specific lineage expansions or existing Rab proteins may fulfill its role ('Discussion').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: CENP-I is predicted to adopt an α-solenoid fold analogous to β-importin.
source: Because the structure of CENP-I is unknown, we submitted its sequence to the structure prediction servers I-TASSER, Phyre2 and Rosetta (Das and Baker, 2008; Zhang, 2008; Kelley and Sternberg, 2009). The α-solenoid fold of β-karyopherins such as Importin-β was consistently identified as a high-confidence template for CENP-I structural modeling (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows the I-TASSER model of CENP-I compared to Importin-β.

claim: RNAi-based depletion of CENP-M results in the complete disappearance of CENP-I from kinetochores.
source: In line with this expectation, RNAi-based depletion of CENP-M resulted in the complete disappearance of CENP-I from kinetochores (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Figure 4E and 4F show immunofluorescence and quantification demonstrating loss of CENP-I from kinetochores upon CENP-M depletion.

claim: The HIKM complex has a long axis of approximately 14 nm and short axes of approximately 5–7 nm.
source: The HIKM complex has a long axis of ∼14 nm and short axes of ∼5–7 nm, and a rather irregular shape, with a broader 'base' and a 'head' domain from which a prominent 'nose' domain emerges.
evidence: Figure 4C shows the 3D reconstruction of the HIKM complex from electron microscopy.

claim: GST-CENP-ML94A–L163E is unable to precipitate CENP-H, CENP-I, and CENP-K when co-expressed in insect cells.
source: A double point mutant of GST-CENP-M, GST-CENP-ML94A–L163E, was unable to precipitate CENP-H, CENP-I, and CENP-K when co-expressed in insect cells, contrarily to GST-CENP-Mwt (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows GST pull-down experiments demonstrating that the mutant does not bind CENP-I.

claim: GFP-CENP-Mwt co-immunoprecipitates CENP-I, CENP-T and Mis12 from mitotic cells.
source: Precipitates of GFP-CENP-Mwt contained CENP-I, the CCAN subunits CENP-T/W, and the KMN protein Mis12.
evidence: Figure 5D shows co-immunoprecipitation results.

claim: GFP-CENP-ML94A–L163E is unable to establish interactions with CENP-I, CENP-T/W, and Mis12.
source: Conversely, GFP-CENP-ML94A–L163E was unable to establish any of these interactions (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows co-immunoprecipitation results demonstrating lack of interaction.

claim: RNAi-resistant GFP-CENP-Mwt rescues the chromosome alignment defect caused by depletion of endogenous CENP-M.
source: RNAi-resistant GFP-CENP-Mwt localized to kinetochores (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, panels A,B) and rescued the severe chromosome alignment defect caused by the depletion of endogenous CENP-M by RNAi, as well as kinetochore localization of CENP-I, demonstrating the specificity of the RNAi-based depletion of CENP-M.
evidence: Figure 5E shows rescue of chromosome alignment and CENP-I localization by wild-type CENP-M.

claim: GFP-CENP-ML94A–L163E does not rescue chromosome alignment or CENP-I localization.
source: GFP-CENP-ML94A–L163E, on the other hand, did not rescue chromosome alignment or CENP-I localization (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Figure 5E and 5F show that the mutant fails to rescue the phenotype.

claim: GFP-CENP-ML94A–L163E does not localize to kinetochores.
source: Furthermore, GFP-CENP-ML94A–L163E did not localize to kinetochores (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, panel D), indicating that CENP-M and CENP-I are mutually required for kinetochore localization.
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2, panel D shows that the mutant does not localize to kinetochores.

claim: CENP-M and CENP-I are mutually required for kinetochore localization.
source: Furthermore, GFP-CENP-ML94A–L163E did not localize to kinetochores (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, panel D), indicating that CENP-M and CENP-I are mutually required for kinetochore localization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the CENP-M mutant that cannot bind CENP-I also cannot localize to kinetochores.

claim: Depletion of CENP-M does not perturb the kinetochore levels of CENP-C.
source: Depletion of CENP-M did not perturb the kinetochore levels of CENP-C (Figure 6A; see Figure 6E for quantification of fluorescence intensity data for panels A–D).
evidence: Figure 6A and 6E show that CENP-C levels remain normal after CENP-M depletion.

claim: The kinetochore levels of Nsl1 remain largely normal after CENP-M depletion.
source: Consistently with the retention of CENP-C in cells depleted of CENP-M, the kinetochore levels of Nsl1, a subunit of the Mis12 complex, remained largely normal after CENP-M depletion (Figure 6B).
evidence: Figure 6B and 6E show that Nsl1 levels are maintained after CENP-M depletion.

claim: Depletion of CENP-M results in co-depletion of CENP-T/W from kinetochores.
source: Depletion of CENP-M, on the other hand, resulted in co-depletion of CENP-T/W from kinetochores. Importantly, this defect was rescued by GFP-CENP-Mwt but not CENP-ML94A–L163E (Figure 6C).
evidence: Figure 6C and 6E show loss of CENP-T/W from kinetochores upon CENP-M depletion.

claim: Loss of CENP-T/W in CENP-M depleted cells correlates with a severe reduction of the kinetochore levels of Ndc80.
source: In line with the idea that CENP-T/W contributes to recruit the Ndc80 complex to kinetochores, loss of CENP-T/W in CENP-M depleted cells correlated with a severe reduction of the kinetochore levels of Ndc80 (also known as Hec1), a subunit of the Ndc80 complex (Figure 6D).
evidence: Figure 6D and 6E show reduced Ndc80 levels after CENP-M depletion.

claim: Depletion of CENP-C prevents kinetochore localization of CENP-T/W.
source: Indeed, depletion of CENP-C prevented kinetochore localization of CENP-T/W both in interphase (Figure 6F; quantified in Figure 6G) and in mitotis (not shown), whereas depletion of CENP-T/W did not alter CENP-C localization (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: Figure 6F and 6G show that CENP-C depletion prevents CENP-T/W localization.

claim: Depletion of CENP-T/W does not alter CENP-C localization.
source: Indeed, depletion of CENP-C prevented kinetochore localization of CENP-T/W both in interphase (Figure 6F; quantified in Figure 6G) and in mitotis (not shown), whereas depletion of CENP-T/W did not alter CENP-C localization (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: Figure 6F and 6G show that CENP-C levels are maintained after CENP-T/W depletion.

claim: The CENP-T/W/X/S complex binds directly to the HIKM complex.
source: Untagged CENP-T/W/X/S complex (Nishino et al., 2012) bound directly to the HIKM complex and was retained on GST-HIKM beads (Figure 7A. Note that the band corresponding to CENP-X is rather diffuse and poorly visible).
evidence: Figure 7A shows GST pull-down demonstrating direct binding between HIKM and CENP-T/W/X/S.

claim: The CENP-T458–C/W complex is sufficient for interaction with the HIKM complex.
source: Indeed, the CENP-T458–C/W complex was sufficient for an interaction with GST-HIKM (Figure 7C), whereas no binding to GST-HIKM was observed with CENP-S/X in the absence of CENP-T/W (Figure 7D).
evidence: Figure 7C shows that the CENP-T histone-fold domain with CENP-W is sufficient for HIKM binding.

claim: CENP-S/X does not bind to the HIKM complex in the absence of CENP-T/W.
source: Indeed, the CENP-T458–C/W complex was sufficient for an interaction with GST-HIKM (Figure 7C), whereas no binding to GST-HIKM was observed with CENP-S/X in the absence of CENP-T/W (Figure 7D).
evidence: Figure 7D shows no binding between CENP-S/X and HIKM.

claim: CENP-M was initially identified for its high expression in proliferating cells.
source: CENP-M was initially identified for its high expression in proliferating cells, and named accordingly PANE1, for proliferation associated nuclear element 1 (Bierie et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: CENP-M was shown to be closely associated with CENP-A and other CCAN subunits.
source: Subsequently, CENP-M was shown to be closely associated with CENP-A, as well as with CENP-H, CENP-K, CENP-I, CENP-L, CENP-N, and CENP-T (Obuse et al., 2004; Foltz et al., 2006; Izuta et al., 2006; Okada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: RNAi-based depletion of CENP-M caused mis-localization of other CCAN subunits.
source: RNAi-based depletion of CENP-M caused mis-localization of other CCAN subunits, thus pointing to an important role of CENP-M in inner kinetochore stability (Foltz et al., 2006; Okada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: At least six kinetochore proteins contain RWD domains.
source: For instance, at least six kinetochore proteins, including the CCAN subunit CENP-O and CENP-P (respectively orthologs of Mcm21 and Ctf19 of S. cerevisiae), contain RWD domains (Schmitzberger and Harrison, 2012; Petrovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The structure of the Chl4/Iml3 complex revealed structural similarity with bacterial RdgC and TBP.
source: More recently, the structure of the Chl4/Iml3 complex of S. cerevisiae, respectively orthologs of CENP-N and CENP-L, revealed structural similarity with the bacterial recombination-association protein RdgC and with TATA-binding protein TBP (Guo et al., 2013; Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: An invariant feature of CENP-M is the presence of leucine at position 52 (of HsCENP-M), equivalent to Gln61 of Ras.
source: An invariant feature of CENP-M is the presence of leucine at position 52 (of HsCENP-M), equivalent to Gln61 (Q61) at the end of the Switch II region of Ras (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutation of Gln61 to Leu in Ras impairs GTP hydrolysis and unleashes the transforming potential of Ras.
source: Mutation of Gln61 to Leu impairs GTP hydrolysis (Scheidig et al., 1999) and unleashes the transforming potential of Ras.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: A substantially conserved P-loop is present in distant CENP-M family members.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, a substantially conserved P-loop is present in distant CENP-M family members (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel E).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel E shows an alignment of distant CENP-M orthologs.

claim: CENP-M cannot be identified in several representatives of Opisthokonta.
source: Interestingly, CENP-M can only be identified in metazoans but not in fungal genomes. Conversely, the other components of the complex, CENP-H, CENP-I, and CENP-K, are nearly ubiquitously conserved and are clearly identified in fungi, where they appear to interact (Measday et al., 2002). Given the importance of CENP-M in kinetochore assembly and stability, and its interaction with evolutionarily conserved proteins, its absence in several representatives of Opisthokonta is puzzling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: It is unlikely that the fission yeast protein Mis17 is a CENP-M ortholog.
source: We consider it unlikely that the fission yeast protein Mis17 is a CENP-M ortholog, as recently proposed (Shiroiwa et al., 2011), because all computational prediction tools we tested failed to identify a domain related to GTPases in Mis17 (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on computational analysis.

claim: Mis17 may act as a functional analogue of CENP-M.
source: It is possible, however, that Mis17 acts as a functional analogue of CENP-M.
evidence: This is speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: A functional GTPase might take up the function of CENP-M in organisms where CENP-M cannot be identified.
source: It is also legitimate to speculate that a functional GTPase, possibly a Rab-family GTPase given its evolutionary proximity to CENP-M, might take up the function of CENP-M in those organisms in which CENP-M cannot be identified.
evidence: This is speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: CENP-C and CENP-T/W have been proposed to create independent connections between centromeres and outer kinetochores.
source: CENP-C and CENP-T/W may create independent connections between centromeres and outer kinetochores.
evidence: Figure 1A shows a schematic of kinetochore organization with this proposed model.

claim: CENP-C binds directly to CENP-A and the Mis12 complex.
source: CENP-C binds directly to CENP-A and Mis12 complex (Przewloka et al., 2011; Screpanti et al., 2011; Kato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1A legend with citations.

claim: CENP-T, together with CENP-W, S and X, may form a nucleosome-like structure interacting directly with DNA and the Ndc80 complex.
source: CENP-T, together with CENP-W, S and X, may form a nucleosome-like structure interacting directly with DNA and the Ndc80 complex (Hori et al., 2008a; Gascoigne et al., 2011; Schleiffer et al., 2012; Nishino et al., 2013, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1A legend with citations.

claim: The KMN network is the main constituent of the outer kinetochore.
source: The KMN network is the main constituent of the outer kinetochore (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction.

claim: The KMN network is a 10-subunit assembly originating from the interaction of three sub-complexes: Knl1-complex, Mis12-complex, and Ndc80-complex.
source: It is a 10-subunit assembly originating from the interaction of three sub-complexes, named the Knl1-complex, the Mis12-complex, and the Ndc80-complex (Cheeseman and Desai, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation.

claim: The KMN network provides at least two sites for microtubule attachment, positioned in the Ndc80 and Knl1 subunits.
source: It provides at least two sites for microtubule attachment, positioned in the Ndc80 and Knl1 subunits, and it regulates cell cycle progression through the recruitment, activation, and subsequent silencing of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) (Foley and Kapoor, 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation.

claim: The inner kinetochore controls outer kinetochore assembly.
source: The inner kinetochore controls outer kinetochore assembly (Liu et al., 2006; McClelland et al., 2007; Cheeseman et al., 2008), influences microtubule binding (McClelland et al., 2007; Amaro et al., 2010), and contributes to epigenetic specification of centromeres (Takahashi et al., 2000; Okada et al., 2006, 2009; Hori et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: CENP-A is a variant of histone H3.
source: The inner kinetochore is built on centromeres, genetic loci whose hallmark is the presence of CENP-A, a variant of histone H3.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction.

claim: CENP-A interacts with histones H2A, H2B and H4 in a nucleosome-like structure.
source: CENP-A interacts with histone H2A, H2B and H4 in a nucleosome-like structure whose precise organization is under discussion (Black and Cleveland, 2011; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation.

claim: The CCAN consists of at least 16 inner kinetochore proteins in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, a group of at least 16 inner kinetochore proteins, collectively identified as constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN), neighbors the CENP-A nucleosome (Obuse et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2005; Foltz et al., 2006; Izuta et al., 2006; Okada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The CCAN interacts with the outer kinetochore and contributes to maintain centromere identity by participating in CENP-A loading.
source: The CCAN (whose subunits are indicated as 'CENP'—for centromeric protein—followed by a letter, see Figure 1A) interacts with the outer kinetochore and contributes to maintain centromere identity by participating in CENP-A loading at every new cell division cycle (Perpelescu and Fukagawa, 2011; Westhorpe and Straight, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The CENP-O/P/Q/U complex has been implicated in microtubule binding and spindle checkpoint control.
source: First, the 4-subunit CENP-O/P/Q/U complex (also known as COMA complex in S. cerevisiae) has been implicated in microtubule binding and spindle checkpoint control (Perpelescu and Fukagawa, 2011), and is believed to interact with CENP-R, a protein of unknown function (Hori et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The CENP-N/L complex binds directly to the CATD box of CENP-A.
source: Second, the 2-subunit CENP-N/L complex binds directly to the CATD box, a specific segment of CENP-A that has been implicated in the epigenetic specification of centromeres (Carroll et al., 2009; Black and Cleveland, 2011; Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The CENP-T/W/S/X complex contains proteins with histone-fold domains that bind DNA.
source: Third, the 4-subunit CENP-T/W/S/X complex contains proteins with histone-fold domains that bind DNA and have been proposed to form a nucleosome-like structure (Hori et al., 2008a; Nishino et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: CENP-C and CENP-T/W interact directly with the Mis12 and Ndc80 complexes, respectively.
source: CENP-C and CENP-T/W interact directly with the Mis12 and Ndc80 complexes, respectively (Gascoigne et al., 2011; Przewloka et al., 2011; Screpanti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: CENP-C provides additional important scaffolding functions, as it binds directly to the CENP-A nucleosome and to the CENP-N/L complex.
source: CENP-C provides additional important scaffolding functions, as it binds directly to the CENP-A nucleosome and to the CENP-N/L complex (Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013; Kato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: Several interactions among CCAN subunits have been recognized in S. cerevisiae and S. pombe, suggesting a conserved plan of kinetochore assembly.
source: Several of these interactions among CCAN subunits have been recognized in S. cerevisiae and in S. pombe, suggesting a conserved plan of kinetochore assembly (Cheeseman et al., 2002; Measday et al., 2002; De Wulf, 2003; Pidoux et al., 2003; Pot et al., 2003; Westermann et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2005; Tanaka et al., 2009; Westermann and Schleiffer, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: CENP-H, CENP-I and CENP-K were proposed to form a complex based on similar chromosome alignment and kinetochore assembly defects after RNAi-based depletions.
source: Because similar chromosome alignment and kinetochore assembly defects were observed after their RNAi-based depletions, CENP-H, CENP-I and CENP-K were proposed to form a complex (Okada et al., 2006; McClelland et al., 2007; Cheeseman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: CENP-M was tentatively assigned as a subunit of the CENP-L/N complex.
source: Conversely, CENP-M was classified in a distinct phenotypic class, and tentatively assigned as a subunit of the CENP-L/N complex (Okada et al., 2006; Westhorpe and Straight, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: CENP-M is required for chromosome alignment and successful mitotic progression.
source: Thus, CENP-M is required for chromosome alignment and successful mitotic progression.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Results section based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: CENP-M does not interact with a collection of recombinant proteins or protein complexes covering most known inner and outer kinetochore proteins or protein complexes.
source: No interaction of CENP-M with a collection of recombinant proteins or protein complexes covering most known inner and outer kinetochore proteins or protein complexes was observed (summarized in Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 lists all the tested interactions, all of which were negative.

claim: The CENP-H/K complex forms a 1:1 dimer.
source: CENP-H/K forms a 1:1 dimer (∼61 kDa) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel B) but elutes near the 158 kDa marker, indicative of an elongated complex.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel B shows static light scattering analysis confirming 1:1 stoichiometry.

claim: The CENP-H/K complex is elongated.
source: CENP-H/K forms a 1:1 dimer (∼61 kDa) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel B) but elutes near the 158 kDa marker, indicative of an elongated complex.
evidence: The SEC elution position is compared to the molecular weight to infer shape.

claim: Both CENP-H/K and CENP-M contribute to CENP-I solubility and stabilization.
source: In summary, these observations suggest that CENP-I bridges CENP-H/K and CENP-M, and that both CENP-H/K and CENP-M contribute to CENP-I solubility and stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CENP-I is only soluble when co-expressed with both CENP-H/K and CENP-M.

claim: The crystal structure of CENP-M1–171 was determined to a resolution of 1.5 Å.
source: We generated crystals of residues 1–171 of CENP-M (a fragment identified by limited proteolysis) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel A) and determined their crystal structure by the SAD (single-wavelength anomalous diffraction) method to a resolution of 1.5 Å using a SeMet derivative (Table 2).
evidence: Table 2 shows crystallographic data collection and refinement statistics.

claim: Rab proteins are the closest structural homologs of CENP-M.
source: Structural superposition with representative members of different families identified Rab proteins as the closest structural homologs of CENP-M (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows structural superpositions and RMSD values.

claim: The switch I region is effectively removed in CENP-M due to a deletion of the entire α1-β2 loop and the β2 strand.
source: A deletion of the entire α1-β2 loop and the β2 strand effectively removed the switch I region (Figure 3C), while the sequence corresponding to switch II (DxxG motif) is highly divergent.
evidence: Figure 3C shows the sequence alignment highlighting these deletions.

claim: The 3D reconstruction of the HIKM complex from negatively stained particles was determined to approximately 22 Å resolution.
source: We determined the three-dimensional (3D) structure of the HIKM complex by negative stain electron microscopy and single particle analysis (Figure 4B,C). The resulting map (Figure 4C) extended to a maximal resolution of 22 Å (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 3, panel C shows the FSC curve used to estimate resolution.

claim: The HIKM complex has an irregular shape with a broader 'base' and a 'head' domain from which a prominent 'nose' domain emerges.
source: The HIKM complex has a long axis of ∼14 nm and short axes of ∼5–7 nm, and a rather irregular shape, with a broader 'base' and a 'head' domain from which a prominent 'nose' domain emerges.
evidence: Figure 4C shows the 3D reconstruction with these features labeled.

claim: Mutation of L94 and L163 did not affect the solubility of CENP-M.
source: Mutation of L94 and L163 did not affect the solubility of CENP-M, nor its behavior during the purification procedure (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows SEC profiles of wild-type and mutant CENP-M.

claim: The CENP-M binding surface is required to establish interactions with other kinetochore proteins.
source: Thus, the CENP-I binding surface of CENP-M is required to establish interactions with other kinetochore proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the CENP-M mutant that cannot bind CENP-I also cannot bind CENP-T/W or Mis12.

claim: CENP-C is required for recruitment of the HIKM complex.
source: Because CENP-C is required for recruitment of the HIKM complex (Milks et al., 2009; Carroll et al., 2010; Gascoigne et al., 2011), and HIKM is in turn required for CENP-T recruitment (this study), we tested and confirmed the prediction that CENP-T recruitment is also dependent on CENP-C.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations and is supported by data in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Disruption of the CENP-M/CENP-I interaction did not have major effects on the kinetochore localization of CENP-C.
source: Conversely, disruption of the CENP-M/CENP-I interaction, or depletion of CENP-T, did not have major effects on the kinetochore localization of CENP-C, as previously suggested (Goshima et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: Figure 6A and 6E show that CENP-C levels are maintained after CENP-M depletion.

claim: The interaction of CENP-C with CENP-A, possibly together with the interaction of CENP-L/N with CENP-A, represents the apex of the CCAN recruitment pathway.
source: These findings unequivocally position CENP-T/W downstream of CENP-C, as previously proposed (Carroll et al., 2010), and imply that the interaction of CENP-C with CENP-A, possibly together with the interaction of CENP-L/N with CENP-A, represents the apex of the CCAN recruitment pathway (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the dependency data.

claim: The CENP-T/W complex interacts directly with the HIKM complex.
source: Collectively, these results clarify that the CENP-T/W complex interacts directly with the HIKM complex, whose subunits are required for the recruitment of the CENP-T/W complex to kinetochores.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by pull-down experiments in Figure 7.

claim: The subunits of the HIKM complex are required for the recruitment of the CENP-T/W complex to kinetochores.
source: Collectively, these results clarify that the CENP-T/W complex interacts directly with the HIKM complex, whose subunits are required for the recruitment of the CENP-T/W complex to kinetochores.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6C.

source: CENP-I (known as Mis6 and Ctf3 in S. pombe and S. cerevisiae, respectively [Saitoh et al., 1997; Measday et al., 2002; Nishihashi et al., 2002])
